paragraphs: In Newport, the city council's fostering service works under the Foster Wales name, alongside the agencies listed on this page. It describes itself as a not-for-profit service and says almost anyone can apply to foster.

The council already looks after most of its children in care through its own fostering arrangements. In May 2025 local democracy reporting said 86% of Newport's more than 300 looked-after children were cared for this way, and that the council planned to move away from independent providers over five years, in line with the Welsh Government's aim of removing profit from children's care. Under that national plan, children in Wales are not to be placed with profit-making providers from April 2030 except in exceptional circumstances, so it is worth asking any agency here whether it is a not-for-profit organisation.

Foster Wales Newport says its allowances depend on the type of fostering, how many children you look after and for how long, and gives the example of carers in the city receiving £660 a week for fostering two children aged four and eight. Its support includes an experienced supervising social worker, mentoring from local foster carers, a peer group for men who foster, get-togethers arranged by children's age group, free gym and swimming for the whole fostering household, and paid membership of The Fostering Network and AFKA.

Becoming a carer starts with a call or enquiry and an information pack, then a home visit, preparation training, an assessment with a social worker and a recommendation from the fostering panel, ending with a foster care agreement. Talk to two or three services before you decide.
